test_title: RRB Group D Previous Year Paper (Held on: 18 Aug 2022 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: To connect a number of resistors in parallel can be considered equivalent to:

options.text: increasing cross sectional area of the conductor
decreasing cross sectional area of the conductor

solution:
The correct answer is __**option 1 ) increasing cross-sectional area of the conductor**__

In a parallel arrangement of resistors, each resistor has its own separate path for current flow, which is analogous to increasing the cross-sectional area of the conductor. This reduces the overall resistance and allows more current to flow through the circuit, similar to what would happen if you used a larger conductor with greater cross-sectional area.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In a series combination, total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances, **and the conductor's cross-sectional area doesn't directly impact the total resistance.**
 
• In a parallel combination, the total resistance depends on the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances, and the **conductor's cross-sectional area can indirectly affect the total resistance by influencing the resistance of the conductor itself,** which may be relevant in practical applications.
 
• Larger cross-sectional areas lead to lower resistance and higher current capacity.
 
• While smaller cross-sectional areas result in higher resistance and lower current capacity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__** 

**The cross-sectional area of a conductor can significantly affect the current passing through it.** 

This relationship is described by **Ohm's Law,** which states that the current (I) flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the cross-sectional area (A) of the conductor and inversely proportional to the resistance (R) of the conductor:

I ∝ (A)/(R)

 To find the total resistance (Rₜₒₜₐₗ) in a series circuit, you simply add up the individual resistances:

 

Rₜₒₜₐₗ = R1 + R2 + R3 + ...

In Parallel combination, the reciprocal of the total resistance (1/Rₜₒₜₐₗ) is equal to the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances:

 

frac{1}R = (1)/(R1) + (1)/(R2) +(1)/(R3) + ...

 [IMAGE: https://th.bing.com/th/id/OIP.5QjY57Y5eiNolDFQDOVXxwHaDz?w=348&h=179&c=7&r=0&o=5&dpr=1.4&pid=1.7] 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

**Resistivity (ρ, rho) is an intrinsic property of a material that quantifies its ability to resist the flow of electric current. It is specific to the material and is measured in ohm-meters (Ω·m).** [IMAGE: https://pressbooks.bccampus.ca/collegephysics/wp-content/uploads/sites/29/2016/04/Figure_21_03_01a.jpg] 

 

Resistivity is a key factor in determining the resistance of a conductor. The resistance of a conductor (R) can be calculated using the formula: R = ρfrac{ L} { A} where ρ is the resistivity, L is the length of the conductor, and A is the cross-sectional area.
